column1: # title: ENG-205 Canterbury Analysis — 3 Numbers & Formulas

column2: The Wife opens by claiming "Experience, though no authority / Were in this world, is right enough for me / To speak of woe that is in mariage."
She has had five husbands at the church door since she was twelve years of age.
Against limits on remarriage she cites "God bade us for to wax and multiply," a "gentil text" she says she understands.
Against clerks who gloss sex organs as for urine only, she answers "Th'experience woot well it is not so."
After the fight Jankin gives her "all the bridle," governance of house and land and of his tongue and hand, and she gets "by maistrye all the sovereinetee."
The knight's life-saving answer is that "Women desire to have sovereignty / As well over their husband as their love, / And for to been in maistrye him above."
The knight puts himself in her "wise governaunce," and she replies that she has got of him "maistry" since she may choose and govern as she likes.
Once given that choice she becomes "bothe fair and good," and she "obeyed him in everything / That might do him plesance," so they live in "parfit joy."
The Prioress "pained her to countrefete cheere / Of court, and to been estatlich of manere, / And to been holden digne of reverence."
Her gold brooch bears a crowned A and the motto "Amor vincit omnia," love conquers all.
After the Monk dismisses cloister texts, the narrator says "And I said his opinion was good," suppressing moral judgment so readers must find the irony.
